extracted.intended_audience: students, scholars, and policymakers interested in democracy, public opinion, and political theory
extracted.subtask_description: Analytic criteria and standards for judging democratic institutions and proposals (e.g., guild socialism, functional representation, legislative practice), focused on how information, representation, coercion, and institutions affect the quality of government.

rubrics_metrics.name: Need for controlled reporting and objective analysis
rubrics_metrics.description: Since the real effects of most laws are subtle and hidden, they cannot be understood by filtering local experiences through local states of mind. They can be known only by controlled reporting and objective analysis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Lawmakers need systematic, empirically grounded reporting and analysis (not merely anecdotes or local impressions) — analogous to an accountant examining cost sheets rather than relying on foremen's testimony. Anti-patterns: relying on fragmented local stories or intuition to judge national policy effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instruments to calibrate local impressions
rubrics_metrics.description: Unless the lawmaker possesses instruments for calibrating local pictures, one picture is as good as the next, and a great deal better.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutional tools (data collection, standardized reports, expert analyses) that translate diverse local inputs into comparable, calibrated information. Avoid treating uncalibrated local impressions as equivalent evidence for national policymaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple unbiased and transparent sources of information
rubrics_metrics.description: The President tells Congress what he chooses to tell it; he cannot be heckled, and the censorship as to what is compatible with the public interest is in his hands.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure legislative information comes from varied, transparent sources (executive, independent expert bodies, private data collected openly). Anti-patterns: exclusive reliance on executive messaging, private tips, or ad hoc revelations that produce incomplete or biased legislative knowledge.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutionalized expert bodies and accessible data for legislators
rubrics_metrics.description: In any consciously organized government, information and analysis suitable for decision should be easily available in a form suitable for decision; where absent, Congressmen must dig for information themselves.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide standing expert agencies, commissions, and data repositories to support informed lawmaking. The presence of organizations like the Interstate Commerce Commission or Federal Trade Commission is given as a positive example; absence leads to incestuous opinion and ineffective legislation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoidance/mitigation of logrolling and parochialism
rubrics_metrics.description: For a legislature without effective means of information and analysis must oscillate between blind regularity, tempered by occasional insurgency, and logrolling. And it is the logrolling which makes the regularity palatable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional designs should limit vote-trading and the bundling of local favors (pork) that distort national policy. Monitor and create incentives to prioritize translocal reasoning over narrow district benefits.

rubrics_metrics.name: Transparency and accountability where coercive powers exist
rubrics_metrics.description: Mr. Cole enumerates many powers of the Commune (fixing prices, allocating resources, levying taxes, appointing judges, controlling armed forces); yet if an entity holds coercive powers, it effectively is a sovereign with coercive authority.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Any body possessing coercive powers must be openly constituted, constrained, and accountable; claims that such a body is 'non-coercive' should be scrutinized. Anti-patterns: concealing or euphemizing coercive authority while leaving it unchecked.

rubrics_metrics.name: Explicit, realistic account of transition mechanisms
rubrics_metrics.description: It is acknowledged that the new society cannot be brought into existence by universal consent; Mr. Cole is too honest to shirk the element of force required to make the transition, and he is clear there would have to be a period of direct action by the trade unions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Political proposals must specify how transitions from one regime to another would occur, including risks of coercion or civil conflict. Beware proposals that ignore or downplay the means of enactment and enforcement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic unit should be a familiar environment (small enough for direct knowledge)
rubrics_metrics.description: This democracy if it is to be real, must come home to, and be exercisable directly by, every individual member of the Guild. The factory (shop) is the natural and fundamental unit of industrial democracy: a workplace small enough to be known directly to all the workers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design representation around units where members can form informed, direct judgments (e.g., shop-level bodies). However, recognize limits: what is 'internal' to such units may be ambiguously defined and constrained by external relations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representation must handle external/entangled relations
rubrics_metrics.description: The unit of industrial democracy is thoroughly entangled in foreign affairs. It is the management of these external relations that constitutes the test of the guild socialist theory.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure mechanisms exist for aggregating, coordinating, and informing local units about issues that transcend their direct experience (industry-wide, regional, national matters). Anti-patterns: treating local self-government as sufficient for complex translocal questions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functional representation requires clear definition and justification of 'functions'
rubrics_metrics.description: The guildsmen imagine a society in which the main work has been analysed into functions; the peculiar virtue of functional democracy is that men vote according to functions in which they are interested. But the scheme of functions cannot be assumed obvious.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If using functional representation, carefully define what counts as a 'function' and how functions are identified and institutionalized. Avoid assuming that functions will be self-evident or that interests alone can reliably delineate them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representatives must be accountable to the functional will, not only to expressed local interest
rubrics_metrics.description: Representatives speak not for the men in the shops, but for certain functions in which the men are interested; they are disloyal if they do not carry out the will of the group about the function, as understood by the group.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design accountability mechanisms so functional delegates are required to represent the considered, informed will regarding a function, not merely immediate or parochial impulses. Consider education, deliberative procedures, and reporting duties to clarify the group's 'will' about a function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Institutional safeguards for uninstructed voters and against machine manipulation
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two kinds of uninstructed voter: one who knows he does not know (and waives his right), and one who does not know that he is uninstructed (whose vote can be mobilized by party machinery).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Electoral and participatory systems should not assume nonparticipation of the uninstructed will safeguard against manipulation. Provide civic education, neutral information channels, and institutional checks against mobilization of uninstructed voters by partisan machines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Functions should not be defined solely by government fiat without legitimacy
rubrics_metrics.description: If you are going to have the government (commune) define functions, the premise of the theory disappears; it had to suppose that a scheme of functions was obvious in order that the concave shops would voluntarily relate themselves to society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure that any top-down assignment of functional categories carries democratic legitimacy and mechanisms for contestation or revision. If functions are imposed, the justificatory basis of functional representation collapses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democracy requires institutions and education to make specialized information common property
rubrics_metrics.description: In the absence of institutions and education by which the environment is so successfully reported that the realities of public life stand out sharply against self-centered opinion, the common interests very largely elude public opinion entirely, and can be managed only by a specialized class.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build public institutions for reporting, analysis, and civic education so that complex, translocal realities are accessible to the public; otherwise governance will depend on an unaccountable specialized class acting on non-shared information.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evaluate governance by processes and results, not only by origin of power
rubrics_metrics.description: The democratic fallacy: preoccupation with the origin of government rather than with the processes and results. The crucial interest is in how power is exercised—the use made of power—not merely in how it was derived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assessment of political systems should emphasize transparency of decision-making, effectiveness, fairness, and tangible results (order, prosperity, rights), not only whether power originated from a democratic source.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid making vital decisions invisible by over-focusing on source-control
rubrics_metrics.description: If you try to control government wholly at the source, you inevitably make all the vital decisions invisible... the men who actually exercise power... exercise power according to opinions which are hidden from the electorate.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design institutions that make substantive decision-making visible and open to scrutiny (procedural transparency, reporting, oversight), rather than only legitimizing the source of power while hiding its exercise.

rubrics_metrics.name: Representatives need systematic data and analysis beyond local experience
rubrics_metrics.description: The worker's opinion of what is right in the great complicated environment out of sight is more likely to be wrong than right if it is a generalization from the experience of the individual shop.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equip representatives with access to comprehensive data, cross-jurisdictional analyses, and expert interpretation so they can make informed judgments on matters beyond their immediate experience; do not rely solely on extrapolation from local knowledge.
